q: A doctor plots patient cases on a map to check whether a suspected water source explains an outbreak. Which visualization goal is this?
e: You already have a guess (the water source) and use the picture to test it, like John Snow's cholera map.

q: A journalist designs a chart so readers instantly grasp how many soldiers died of disease versus wounds. Which goal is this?
e: The insight is already known; the chart's job is to get it across to an audience (like Nightingale's diagrams).

q: An analyst explores a migration dataset with no specific question, looking for patterns worth investigating. Which goal fits best?
e: Open-ended exploration to support reasoning, rather than testing a specific guess or presenting a finished message.

q: Sketching a specimen or photographing motion frames (like Muybridge's horse) mainly serves which goal?
e: Recording captures information so it can be kept and studied later.

q: Why is finding the most frequent number faster in a bar chart than in a grid of numbers?
a: Perception spots it in parallel, without counting
w: Bar charts contain more data than tables do
Tables can't store repeated values properly
Numbers are harder to print clearly than bars
e: Perception does the work in parallel instead of reading and counting values one by one. Visualization offloads work from limited cognition and working memory onto fast visual perception.

q: Visualization 'enhances working memory' mainly because:
a: The picture serves as external memory
w: It permanently boosts how much you remember
It removes the need to look at the data
It compresses the data into fewer values
e: The picture acts as external memory you can look back at instead of holding values in your head. Like doing multiplication on paper, the display stores intermediate information for you.

q: The lecture warns that perception can point out interesting things 'but can also deceive you.' What's the practical lesson?
a: Design choices can create patterns that aren't there
w: Visualization should be avoided for big decisions
Only statistics can be trusted, never charts
Perception is too slow to use on large datasets
e: Design choices can create patterns that aren't in the data, so encodings must be chosen carefully. The same power that makes patterns pop out can make false patterns pop out.

q: Anscombe argued computers should produce both calculations and graphs. What's the main reason?
a: Identical statistics can hide very different data
w: Graphs are always more accurate than statistics
Calculations are too slow to run without graphs
Graphs have replaced the need for statistics
e: Datasets with identical summary statistics can look completely different when plotted. Summary statistics can hide structure (outliers, curves, clusters) that a plot reveals.

q: Because only the fovea sees sharply and the eye jumps between fixations, what design advice follows?
a: Don't cram too much on screen; keep it crisp
w: Show as much detail as possible; the eye scans it all
Put the key information at the edges of the screen
Use blur to pull attention away from the center
e: Avoid cramming too much data on screen; crisp, clear visuals are interpreted best. We only see a small area in detail at a time, and the brain fills in the rest.

q: Your brain 'fills in' the blind spot and peripheral blur. What does this imply for reading a visualization?
a: Viewers may think they saw details they didn't
w: Viewers always notice every mark on the chart
Peripheral vision is best for reading labels
The blind spot only matters for 3D charts
e: Viewers may believe they saw details they never actually looked at. Vision is limited at any moment; the brain reconstructs the rest.

q: Mach bands and the Cornsweet illusion show that the visual system mainly responds to:
w: The average color of a region
e: Edges and differences, not absolute brightness. Receptive fields enhance edges, so perceived brightness depends on contrast at boundaries.

q: If the outlines of shapes are important in your chart, the lecture advises you to:
w: Match the shape color to the background
e: Since we're tuned to edges, strong contrast makes boundaries clear.

q: Weber's law says we judge relative differences. Which comparison is EASIEST?
a: Two bars on a common baseline, side by side
w: Two bars on different baselines, far apart
Two unaligned bars of nearly equal length
Two circles of slightly different areas
e: Two bars sitting on a common baseline next to each other. Aligning items on a common axis turns the judgment into a small, relative difference that's easy to see.

q: Two identical gray squares look different because one sits on a dark background and one on a light one. This is:
e: Judgments of brightness and color are relative to the local surroundings.

q: Given simultaneous contrast, what should you do when encoding values with gray levels or color?
a: Keep marks on a neutral, uniform background
w: Use a rainbow background to boost contrast
Put each mark on a different colored background
Rely on viewers to judge absolute brightness
e: Avoid placing marks on varying or busy backgrounds; keep the context neutral. Do your best not to place data in difficult contexts; choose position and background carefully.

q: You want one important point to stand out among hundreds. Which approach works best?
a: Make it differ in a single strong channel, like a unique color
w: Make it differ in both color and shape from different distractors
Make it slightly larger than the rest
Hide it among similar shapes with a label
e: Popout works on one strong feature contrast; conjunctions of features need slow serial search.

q: A target is the only red circle among red squares and blue circles. Why is it slow to find?
a: It's a conjunction, so it needs serial search
w: Red is a weak channel for pre-attentive search
Circles are a shape that can never pop out
There are too few distractors on the screen
e: It's a conjunction of features, which requires serial search instead of popping out. Each distractor shares one feature with the target, so no single channel separates it.

q: What matters most for something to pop out pre-attentively?
a: Strong contrast with the surrounding features
w: The total number of colors that are used
The overall size of the whole chart
Whether the viewer has read the legend
e: Strong contrast between the target's feature and the surrounding features. Pop-out depends on feature contrast, not on how much is on screen.

q: Why should color and shape be used sparingly for highlighting?
a: If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out
w: Color is slow for the eye to perceive
Many shapes are hard to print clearly
Browsers limit how many colors can be shown
e: Popout depends on contrast with everything else; overusing it destroys that contrast.

q: In a scatterplot, you draw a box around a cluster of points to show they belong together. Which Gestalt principle are you using?
e: Elements inside a common boundary are perceived as a group.

q: A line chart connects each country's yearly points with a line, so we read them as one series. Which principle?
e: Visually connected elements are perceived as related, and connection is a very strong grouping cue.

q: Using the same color for all bars belonging to one category relies on:
e: Things that look alike (color, size, shape) are perceived as related.

q: Leaving extra space between groups of bars in a grouped bar chart uses which principle?
e: Items close together are seen as a group; gaps separate groups.

q: In an animated chart, points that move together are seen as a cluster. Which principle?
e: Elements moving in the same direction are perceived as a unit.

q: A line passes behind a label, but viewers still see one continuous line. Which principle?
e: We complete hidden objects into simple, familiar shapes.

q: A busy background makes it unclear which marks are data and which are decoration. Which principle is being violated?
e: Elements are perceived as either figure or background; data should clearly be the figure.

q: What's the risk of using Gestalt principles carelessly?
a: Viewers may see relationships that aren't there
w: The charts will render much more slowly
The colors will look washed out on screen
Viewers will start to ignore the legend
e: Viewers may see groupings or relationships that aren't in the data. Poor use may cause users to see things that aren't there.

q: You're tuning a chart color by hand and want to make it 'less vivid' without changing what color it is. Which model makes that easiest?
e: HSV is more intuitive for tuning: hue = which color, saturation = how much white, value/lightness = how much black.

q: Why is RGB a poor space for building a colormap where equal steps should look equally different?
w: It only works for print media
It has too few colors to use
e: It isn't perceptually uniform, and the actual color depends on the device. Equal numeric steps in RGB don't produce equal perceived steps.

q: Which color space is designed so distances roughly match perceived differences?
e: LAB is mathematically defined and perceptually based: L* lightness, a red–green, b yellow–blue.

q: Printing a chart on paper uses which kind of color mixing?
e: Ink absorbs light, so print is subtractive; K gives a true black.

q: In HSV terms, a pastel color is one with:
e: Low saturation (more white mixed in). Saturation is the amount of white mixed in; pastels have little saturation.

q: A chart uses red for 'loss' and green for 'gain' and nothing else. What's the main accessibility problem?
a: Common color deficiencies confuse red and green
w: Red and green both print poorly on paper
Red always means danger to every viewer
Green has low luminance contrast with white
e: The most common color deficiencies make red and green hard to tell apart. Deuteranomaly (most common) and protanomaly both impair red–green discrimination.

q: Which fix best makes a red/green chart readable for colorblind viewers?
a: Also vary luminance or add shape or labels
w: Make the red and the green more saturated
Switch the chart over to a rainbow colormap
Use a much darker background behind the marks
e: Also vary luminance or add a second cue like shape or labels. Design with colorblindness in mind: vary hue, saturation and brightness, or use cues besides color.

q: Maureen Stone's advice 'get it right in black and white' means:
a: It should still work with color removed
w: Always publish charts only in grayscale
Avoid using white backgrounds in any chart
Black-and-white printers are the target audience
e: The chart should still work if color is removed, so luminance carries the key structure. If it works without hue, luminance differences are doing the heavy lifting, which also helps colorblind viewers.

q: You need fine detail (thin lines, small text) to be readable. Which channel should carry it?
e: Luminance (light vs. dark contrast). We have higher contrast sensitivity for luminance than for chrominance.

q: Gray text on a slightly lighter gray background is hard to read. What does the lecture's guideline say?
w: Any contrast is fine if the hue differs
Use 1:1 contrast for a clean, elegant look
Contrast only matters for printed text
e: Aim for about 10:1 luminance contrast, never below 3:1. Text needs strong luminance contrast to be legible.

q: Small scatterplot points in pale colors are hard to tell apart. Why?
a: Small marks make colors harder to distinguish
w: Pale colors can't be printed very accurately
Small marks don't really have any hue at all
Scatterplots should never use color for points
e: The smaller the mark, the harder colors are to distinguish. Bertin: color differences shrink with mark size. Use brighter, more saturated colors for small marks.

q: Which saturation choice fits each use: large background areas vs. small points?
a: Pastels for large areas; saturated for small marks
w: Saturated for large areas; pastels for small marks
Pastel colors everywhere, to avoid clutter
e: Low-saturation pastels for large areas; bright, saturated colors for small marks. Large saturated areas are overwhelming; small marks need saturation to be visible.

q: You're coloring countries by political party (5 parties). What kind of colormap fits?
a: Categorical: one distinct hue per party
w: Diverging: two hues centered on zero
Rainbow: a ramp ordered by party size
e: Hue has no inherent order, which suits categorical data. Keep it to about 6–12 hues.

q: You're coloring counties by median income. Which colormap fits?
e: Sequential: vary luminance and/or saturation from low to high. Ordered data needs a channel with an inherent order, like luminance or saturation.

q: You're showing temperature change relative to a baseline, with warmer and cooler values. Which colormap fits?
a: Diverging: two hues around a neutral middle
w: Sequential: one hue from light to dark
Categorical: one distinct hue per value
Rainbow: the full spectrum from red to violet
e: Diverging: two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint for zero change. A diverging map makes the meaningful midpoint (zero change) explicit.

q: Why are rainbow colormaps discouraged for continuous data?
a: Uneven contrast and no natural order
w: They use too few colors to be useful
They only work when printed on paper
They are much too dark on most screens
e: Perceived contrast is uneven and they have no explicit midpoint or natural order. Rainbow creates false boundaries and hides others; people don't agree on its order.

q: A design uses 20 different hues to label 20 categories. What's the problem?
a: People can only tell about 6–12 colors apart
w: Hue can't be used to encode categories at all
20 colors exceed what screens can display
Categorical data always needs luminance instead
e: People can only reliably tell apart about 6–12 colors at once. Beyond about 6–12 hues, categories become confusable; consider grouping or other channels.

q: Why are nameable colors (red, blue, orange) better for categories than subtle shades?
e: They're easier to remember and refer to. Categorical colors are easier to remember if they're nameable.

q: A bivariate colormap mixes two continuous variables into one color. When does this work reasonably?
w: When each one uses a rainbow ramp
Never, under any conditions at all
e: When at least one of the variables is binary. Bivariate colormaps are hard to read unless one variable has only two values.

q: 'Expressiveness' for colormaps means:
a: Match the colormap to the attribute type
w: Use as many distinct colors as possible
Always use the organization's brand palette
Prefer bright, saturated colors for everything
e: Match the colormap type to the attribute type (categorical, sequential, diverging). The colormap should express exactly the structure the data has, no more and no less.

q: A dashboard uses five bright colors equally for everything. What does the 'simplicity' guideline suggest?
a: One base color, with sparing accents
w: Add more colors to balance them out
Make all the colors equally saturated
e: Pick one base color used in larger amounts and use others sparingly for interest. Be selective about the base color and use accents sparingly.

q: When color isn't needed, what does the lecture suggest instead?
a: Neutrals plus channels like size and shape
w: A rainbow colormap, just to be safe
Only shades of red for every mark
Remove all marks and use a table instead
e: Use neutrals and other channels like size, shape or position. Avoidance of color: neutrals work with any scheme, and diagrammatic marks may be better channels.

q: Ordinal data is encoded with color. Where should the marks be placed?
e: Color is relative; a neutral background avoids contrast effects shifting perceived values.

q: Why describe data in abstract terms (items, attributes) instead of domain terms (patients, genes)?
a: It lets design knowledge carry across domains
w: It makes the datasets themselves smaller
It hides the data's meaning from the users
e: It lets you reuse design knowledge across domains and reason systematically about the design space. Abstract vocabulary avoids domain-specific terms, so the what-why-how framework applies anywhere.

q: In the what-why-how framework, choosing between a bar chart and a heatmap is part of:
e: How (the encoding and interaction). What = data, why = the user's task, how = the visual encoding and interaction.

q: A spreadsheet of students with columns for name, age and major. What are the rows and columns?
a: Rows are items; columns are attributes
w: Rows are attributes; columns are items
Rows are links; columns are positions
Rows are grids; columns are fields
e: In a table, each row is an item and each column is an attribute.

q: A social network of friendships between people is which dataset type?
e: Network: items (nodes) connected by links. Networks consist of items (nodes) and links, both of which can have attributes.

q: Wind measurements (speed and direction) at every point of a weather grid are best described as:
e: Fields have values at cells across continuous space; direction plus magnitude is a vector.

q: Temperature measured at every cell of a 3D grid is a field with what kind of attribute?
e: A single number per cell is scalar; direction+magnitude is a vector; a matrix per cell is a tensor.

q: When visualizing a continuous field from sampled points, which two choices shape what viewers see?
e: Sampling (where values are measured) and interpolation (how values in between are modeled). Grid choices affect how continuous data is interpreted.

q: Blood type (A, B, AB, O) is which attribute type?
e: There's no inherent order among blood types.

q: Survey answers 'disagree, neutral, agree' are which attribute type?
e: They have a clear order, but the 'distance' between levels isn't a meaningful number.

q: Height in centimeters is which attribute type?
e: It has a meaningful magnitude, so arithmetic (differences, averages) makes sense.

q: Which test tells ordinal and quantitative apart?
a: Whether arithmetic on the values is meaningful
w: Whether the values can be sorted in some order
Whether the values are written as words or text
Whether there are more than five distinct values
e: Whether arithmetic like differences and averages is meaningful. Both can be ordered; only quantitative data has meaningful magnitudes.

q: Month of the year (Jan … Dec, then back to Jan) is an ordered attribute that is:
e: It wraps around, so the end connects back to the start.

q: Profit, where values range from losses through zero to gains, is an ordered attribute that is:
e: There's a meaningful midpoint (zero) with values going in two directions.

q: You convert exact temperatures into 'hot, warm, cold'. What have you created, and why might you?
w: A field built from a table
e: A derived ordinal attribute that simplifies the data for the task. Derived attributes are computed from the originals; the transformation is an abstraction choice.

q: Turning temperature into 'above freezing / below freezing' produces which attribute type?
e: Two groups with no meaningful magnitude between them.

q: What's the difference between the data model and the conceptual model?
a: The math type vs. what the values mean
w: They are exactly the same thing
The chart vs. the file it's stored in
The database schema vs. the data rows
e: The data model is the math type (e.g., floats); the conceptual model is what the values mean (e.g., temperature). Knowing the meaning (conceptual model) motivates which abstraction to choose.

q: In a scatterplot, what are the marks and what are the channels?
w: Axes; the points that are plotted on them
Colors; the lines drawn between the points
Labels; the grid lines behind the whole plot
e: Points are the marks; horizontal and vertical position are the channels. Marks are graphical elements; channels control their appearance.

q: In a bar chart, what are the marks and which channel encodes the value?
e: Lines (bars) as marks; length/vertical position encodes the value. Each bar is a mark whose length shows the quantity.

q: A choropleth map uses which mark type for regions?
e: Marks are classified by spatial dimension: points 0D, lines 1D, areas 2D.

q: You need to show product categories (no order). Which channel type fits?
a: An identity channel like hue or shape
w: A magnitude channel like bar length
Luminance ramping from light to dark
Area size scaled to the category
e: An identity channel like hue, shape or spatial region. Expressiveness: identity channels for categorical data, magnitude channels for ordered data.

q: Why is encoding a quantitative value with shape a bad idea?
w: Shapes are hard for browsers to draw
Shape is the most accurate channel
Shapes take up too much space
e: Shape has no inherent order or magnitude, so it can't express 'how much'. Shape is an identity channel; it can't convey magnitude.

q: You want viewers to compare values as accurately as possible. Which channel should you use?
e: Position on a common scale is the most effective magnitude channel.

q: Why is a bar chart usually more accurate than a pie chart for comparing values?
a: Length is judged more accurately than angle
w: Bar charts can use more colors than pies
Pie charts can't show percentages at all
Bars are always sorted from high to low
e: Length/position is judged more accurately than angle or area. In the effectiveness ranking, position and length outrank angle and area.

q: Which magnitude channel ranks lowest in effectiveness?
e: Curvature and volume are at the bottom of the ranking.

q: Effectiveness says the most important attribute should get:
w: The least effective channel, to save space
e: Rank attributes by importance and assign the best channels to the most important ones.

q: Channel effectiveness rankings mostly come from:
e: Perception experiments measuring how accurately people judge each channel. Rankings come from studies like Cleveland & McGill and crowdsourced experiments.

q: You encode 15 levels of a variable using line width. What's the concern?
e: Discriminability: viewers can't reliably tell that many widths apart. Each channel supports only a limited number of distinguishable steps.

q: You map one variable to a rectangle's width and another to its height. What happens?
a: They fuse, so people see overall area
w: Each is read independently, with no interference
Width turns into a categorical channel
Height outranks width, so width is ignored
e: They're integral, so viewers see overall area/shape instead of each variable separately. Width and height are integral channels, perceived holistically.

q: Which pair of channels is separable, so each can be read independently?
e: Separable channels can be judged individually; integral ones fuse.

q: A 3D bar chart makes back bars look smaller and hides some behind others. Which problems are these?
w: Low data-ink ratio and chart junk
e: 3D adds perspective cues that interfere with size and color, plus occlusion and poor text legibility.

q: When is animation a GOOD choice?
e: Storytelling and smooth transitions between views. Animation is good for narrative and transitions, bad for detailed comparison.

q: You want readers to compare how 12 regions changed across 10 years. Which is better?
w: An animation, one year at a time
e: Small multiples, so they can compare by moving their eyes. Comparing views side by side uses the display as external memory; animation forces comparison against memory.

q: A chart shows a 20% increase in the data, but the bar grows to look 100% bigger. What's the Lie Factor?
e: 5 (100% ÷ 20%). Lie Factor = size of effect shown in the graphic ÷ size of effect in the data. Ideally it's 1.

q: Icons are scaled by height (diameter) to show values twice as large. What goes wrong?
w: Nothing; scaling by height is exactly right
The difference looks smaller than it really is
The icons lose their color when they're scaled
e: Area grows four times, so the difference looks exaggerated. Area scales with the square of the linear size, so scale by area, not by diameter.

q: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0, making a small change look dramatic. When is a non-zero baseline acceptable?
a: When zero isn't meaningful or it's the norm
w: Always, since it saves a lot of vertical space
Never, under any circumstances or for any chart
Only when the chart is a pie or donut chart
e: When zero isn't meaningful, to show relative position, or where it's the norm (like stock charts). Bars encode length from a baseline, so truncation distorts them unless zero doesn't make sense.

q: A chart shows numbers without any axis or baseline. Why is that a problem?
a: Viewers can't judge the size of differences
w: It uses far too much ink for the data
It reduces the color contrast of the marks
It breaks the Gestalt principle of closure
e: Without a scale or baseline, viewers can't judge the true size of differences. Missing scales hide distortion; clear labeling defeats ambiguity.

q: 'Show data variation, not design variation' warns against:
a: Design changes that look like data changes
w: Using any color at all anywhere in a chart
Showing the real variation that's in the data
Using more than one chart on the same page
e: Changing visual design (like icon size or style) in ways that look like changes in data. Unintended size coding makes design differences read as data differences.

q: A chart shows a stock dropping sharply, but the full history shows it's a small dip. What's missing?
e: Context (a longer time range or comparison). Insufficient context can make normal variation look like a crash.

q: One value is 100× bigger than the rest and squashes everything else flat. Which is a reasonable fix?
a: A log scale or a scale break
w: Switch over to a pie chart
e: Use a log scale or a scale break (or clip it and say so). Clipping, scale breaks and log scales are the lecture's options. Always be transparent.

q: Why use a log scale when data spans several orders of magnitude?
w: It makes all the values look equal
It removes outliers from the data
It makes the chart more colorful
e: Equal distances show equal ratios, so small and large values are both readable. Log scales show multiplicative change and keep small values from being flattened.

q: Removing heavy gridlines, borders and shading while keeping the data is an example of:
e: Data-ink ratio = ink used for data ÷ total ink. Erase non-data ink when it adds nothing.

q: A study found the most minimal box plot (highest data-ink ratio) was hardest to interpret. What's the lesson?
w: Box plots should never be used at all
More decoration is always an improvement
Data-ink ratio has nothing to do with design
e: Maximizing data-ink isn't always best; some 'redundant' ink helps comprehension. The counterpoint shows data-ink is a guideline, not a law.

q: Research on embellished 'chart junk' found it can help with:
e: Long-term memorability and engagement. Embellished charts were recalled better weeks later; the cons are interpretability, trust and space.

q: When is chart junk most defensible?
a: When the goal is memorability or engagement
w: When readers need to read exact values
When space on the page is very limited
When the audience is a team of analysts
e: When the goal is persuasion, memorability or engagement rather than careful analysis. Chart junk? It depends: pros are persuasion, memorability and engagement.

q: Data density = data entries ÷ area of the graphic. How does Tufte suggest increasing it?
e: Shrink the graphics, e.g., with small multiples or sparklines. Show more data in the same space.

q: A trellis plot splits data into a grid of small charts. Which variables usually define the grid?
e: Subdivide by nominal/ordinal variables so each panel compares like with like.

q: A designer adds many extra visual features, assuming viewers will take it all in at once. Which illusion is this?
e: Viewers can't absorb everything at once, and extra features make specific information harder to find.

q: A designer assumes users will look at every part of a dashboard, but they only look where they expect. Which illusion?
e: Users attend to less of the display than designers think.

q: A designer assumes that because users looked at a chart, they understood it fully. Which illusion?
e: Attending to something doesn't mean deep understanding.

q: A 3D pie chart makes a smaller slice in front look bigger than a larger slice behind it. Why?
a: Perspective makes front slices look larger
w: Pie charts can't show percentages at all
The slice colors were far too similar
The chart's legend was missing entirely
e: Perspective distorts slice areas, so front slices look larger. 3D perspective changes apparent size; a flat bar chart avoids it.

q: Why are dual-axis charts risky?
a: Independent scales can fake crossings or trends
w: They use far too much ink for the data shown
They can't show changes over time at all
They require a 3D perspective to draw
e: Each axis can be scaled independently, so lines can be made to cross or diverge to suggest false relationships. The crossing point is an artifact of the chosen scales, not of the data.

q: Tufte's graphical excellence aims to give viewers:
a: The most ideas, fastest, with the least ink and space
w: The most colors in the largest space for impact
The most decoration, to keep viewers engaged
The fewest ideas per chart, for maximum clarity
e: The most ideas, in the shortest time, with the least ink, in the smallest space. It's about efficient communication: as simple as possible, but no simpler.

q: 'Find which states have unusually high unemployment' as an {action, target} pair is:
e: Tasks are abstracted as an action plus a target.

q: A news graphic that tells readers a finished story serves which consume goal?
e: Present = communicate something already known; discover = find new insight; enjoy = casual interest.

q: A researcher uses a tool to find new patterns nobody knew about. Which consume goal?
e: Discover means generating or verifying new hypotheses.

q: A beautiful live wind map people browse just for fun serves which goal?
e: Casual, curiosity-driven use with no specific task.

q: You know the name of the city you're looking for but not where it is on the map. Which search task?
e: Target known, location unknown = locate.

q: You know both what you're looking for and where it is (e.g., a specific cell in a table). Which search task?
e: Target known, location known = lookup.

q: You scan a particular region of a chart without a specific target in mind. Which search task?
e: Location known, target unknown = browse.

q: You have no specific target and don't know where to look. Which search task?
e: Neither target nor location known = explore.

q: You look at one data point, then two, then the whole set. These query actions are:
e: Queries scale from one target, to some, to all.

q: 'Which car has the highest horsepower?' is which low-level task?
e: Find data cases with an extreme value of an attribute.

q: 'What's the average price of houses in this neighborhood?' is which low-level task?
e: It computes a new number from the data.

q: 'Show only movies released after 2010' is which low-level task?
e: Find data cases that satisfy a condition.

q: 'Is there a relationship between study hours and exam score?' is which low-level task?
e: Determine useful relationships between attributes.

q: 'Are there groups of similar customers?' is which low-level task?
e: Find clusters of similar attribute values.

q: 'What's the spread of salaries from lowest to highest?' is which low-level task?
e: Find the span of values for an attribute.

q: Clicking a county on a map highlights the same county in a linked bar chart. Which interaction is this?
e: Linking (brushing across views). Linked views share selections so you can see one item across multiple representations.

q: Dragging a slider to hide all flights shorter than 500 miles is:
e: Filtering removes items that don't meet a condition (e.g., Crossfilter).

q: Zooming into a map makes street names and buildings appear that weren't shown before. This is:
e: Semantic zoom changes what's shown (level of detail); geometric zoom only magnifies.

q: Switching a view from a bar chart to a sorted dot plot is which kind of interaction?
e: Rearranging (changing the encoding). Rearranging changes how the same data is encoded or ordered.

q: Smoothly animating bars to their new positions when the sort order changes helps because:
a: It lets viewers track items as things move
w: Animation shows the exact values clearly
It hides the changes from the viewer
It lowers the chart's data-ink ratio
e: Animated transitions let viewers track items as the view changes. Change over time: transitions preserve context between states.

q: Panning and rotating a view are examples of:
e: Navigation changes the viewpoint (pan, translate, rotate, zoom).
